name: Composio
summary: A hosted tool layer for AI agents: one session per end user gives the model a few meta tools to search, authorize and run actions across more than 1,500 app toolkits, with Composio holding and refreshing the OAuth tokens.
intro: Your code calls `composio.create(user_id)` and gets a session: the user, the toolkits in scope, their connected accounts and a remote sandbox. Instead of loading hundreds of tool definitions into the model’s context, the session hands the model a small fixed set of meta tools. The model searches for a tool such as `GITHUB_CREATE_ISSUE`, asks for a connection if the user has none, and runs it, and every call goes back through `session.execute()` to Composio’s servers, which call the app’s API as that user. Large responses can be written to the session’s sandbox, where the agent filters them with Python rather than pasting them into its context.

Authentication is the part Composio takes off your hands. When a tool needs an account, the `COMPOSIO_MANAGE_CONNECTIONS` meta tool returns a hosted Connect Link; the user signs in there, and Composio stores the token under your `user_id` and refreshes it. Credentials never pass through your app or the model. By default it uses Composio’s own shared OAuth apps; you bring your own app for your branding and scopes. The same session works through provider packages that reshape tools for OpenAI, Anthropic, LangChain and other frameworks, or as a hosted MCP endpoint (`session.mcp.url`) for any MCP client.

The company behind it is Sampark Inc., which does business as Composio. The Python and TypeScript SDKs are MIT-licensed on GitHub, but tool execution, token storage and the toolkit catalog run in Composio’s cloud. The Hobby plan is free with 100,000 tool calls a month; past the free amounts, tool calls cost $0.0003 each, meta tools such as tool search are free, and Pro is $29 a month with that much usage credit included.
strengths: OAuth handled end to end: hosted consent pages, token storage and refresh per user, so the model and your backend never see raw credentials
Context stays small: a handful of meta tools instead of every tool definition, and a sandbox for large results
One session, many front ends: provider packages for common agent frameworks, or the same session as a hosted MCP server
Cheap to start: 100,000 tool calls a month free, then $0.0003 per call, with spend caps on Pro
limits: Every call runs through Composio’s cloud, so it holds your users’ tokens and sees tool traffic; zero data retention and a HIPAA BAA are paid add-ons on Pro
Rate limits are per organization across all endpoints: 2,000 requests a minute on Hobby and 10,000 on Pro

Composio’s shared OAuth apps are the easy default but count against lower allowances (20,000 of the free 100,000 tool calls) and cost an extra $0.0002 per call; scaling means registering your own OAuth apps
The API has moved fast: sessions replaced direct execution in 2026, REST v3.1 changed tool-version defaults, and older “entity”, “action” and “integration” tutorials no longer match the SDK

story: Once language models could call functions, every agent team hit the same chores: write a wrapper for each API, run an OAuth flow for each user and app, store and refresh the tokens, and keep the wrappers working as the APIs changed. Composio, founded in 2023 by Soham Ganatra and Karan Vaidya, with offices in San Francisco and Bengaluru, set out to do that once for everyone, as a catalog of ready-made tools with the authentication handled in its cloud. Its open-source SDK repository on GitHub dates from February 2024.

In mid-2025 Composio rebuilt its platform and released new v3 SDKs, renaming its concepts along the way because, its engineers wrote, users kept asking what an “integration”, a “connection” and an “app” each meant: actions became tools, apps became toolkits, integrations became auth configs and entity IDs became user IDs. In July 2025 Ganatra announced $29 million in total funding, including a $25 million Series A led by Lightspeed Venture Partners, to build “skills that evolve with your agents”, so that what one agent learns about a tool helps every other agent on the platform.

In 2026 the session became the center of the product. A session gives the model meta tools to search for and run tools at runtime, rather than loading every tool definition into context, plus a sandbox for large results; by mid-2026 both SDKs made sessions first-class and older direct execution became a legacy path. New usage-based pricing arrived in August 2026, and in October Composio Instant let agents pay per call for more than 100 paid third-party tools from a prepaid wallet, with no account at the tool’s vendor.

choices.choice: Host the tools and the tokens instead of shipping libraries
choices.why: OAuth consent, token storage and refresh are the parts each team otherwise rebuilds per app; running them centrally lets one Connect Link and one user ID cover every toolkit, and keeps credentials away from the model and the app.

choices.choice: Meta tools that search instead of a full tool list
choices.why: Loading hundreds of tool schemas into a model’s context is slow and confuses it, so a session exposes a small fixed set of tools to discover, authenticate and execute others at runtime.

Composio’s v3 SDK post admits its earlier names collided (is an “integration” the app or one configuration of it?), so it renamed actions, apps, integrations and connections to tools, toolkits, auth configs and connected accounts.

choices.choice: Bill per tool call, with search free
choices.why: Pricing follows what the platform runs: each tool execution counts once, while meta tools such as tool search cost nothing, so letting the model look around is not penalized.
